strategies.rule_text: When a matrix composition function in `astropy/modeling/separable.py` produces incorrect separability results for nested models, inspect each `_cstack`/`_cdot` helper to verify it propagates the actual sub-matrix values rather than replacing them with scalar constants like `1`.

When combining sub-matrices in separability computations, never substitute a sub-matrix with a uniform fill value (e.g., `np.ones` or `= 1`), as this discards the internal structure of nested compound models and makes independent inputs appear coupled.

When adding tests for `separability_matrix` in `astropy/modeling/`, include cases where a `CompoundModel` is itself an operand of another `CompoundModel` (nested `&` or `|`), since flat and nested compositions can exercise different code paths in `_cstack` and `_cdot`.

When tracing a separability bug, follow the recursive call chain from `separability_matrix` → `_separable` → `_cstack`/`_cdot` in `astropy/modeling/separable.py` to identify which composition step corrupts the matrix before looking elsewhere.

When a helper function handles both a plain `Model` input and a pre-computed matrix input via an `isinstance` branch, ensure the matrix branch uses the existing matrix data directly rather than reconstructing it from shape metadata alone, so structural information is not silently lost.

When a format class in `astropy/io/ascii` raises `TypeError` for an unexpected keyword argument, trace the call chain from `ui.py`'s `_get_writer` through the format's `__init__` to find where the parameter needs to be accepted and forwarded to the parent class.

When a subclass hardcodes a line offset (like `start_line = 3`) that depends on the number of header rows, replace it with a dynamic calculation (e.g., `2 + len(self.header.header_rows)`) in the `read` method so the class stays correct when header configuration changes.

When extending a fixed-width format writer in `astropy/io/ascii`, check both the `write` method's line-indexing logic and the `__init__` signature, since both must be updated together to support variable-length headers.

When adding a new keyword argument to an ASCII format class, write tests that cover both reading and writing with the new parameter, verifying that the output line count and separator positions match the expected structure for each `header_rows` combination.

When a `write` method in an ASCII format class uses a hardcoded index (like `lines[1]`) to reference a structural element such as a separator line, replace it with an index derived from the actual header configuration so the logic remains correct as header rows are added or removed.
When parsing user-provided text formats in `astropy/io/ascii`, compile regex patterns with `re.IGNORECASE` so that format parsers don't silently reject valid input that differs only in case.

When comparing string tokens read from a file against known sentinel values (like `"NO"`, `"NAN"`, or command keywords), normalize with `.upper()` or `.lower()` before comparison so case variations don't cause incorrect behavior.

When a `ValueError: Unrecognized QDP line` (or similar "unrecognized input" error) is raised in an ascii reader, trace back to the regex in `_line_type` and check whether the pattern anchors or literals are unintentionally case-sensitive.
When adding case-insensitivity fixes to format parsers in `astropy/io/ascii`, add test cases with mixed-case and lower-case variants of all recognized keywords to prevent regressions.

When investigating parsing bugs in `astropy/io/ascii/qdp.py`, start with `_line_type` and `_get_tables_from_qdp_file` since they own the regex compilation and token comparison logic that controls how every line is classified and interpreted.

When calling string or array transformation methods like `.replace()` on numpy `chararray` objects in `fitsrec.py`, always assign the result back (e.g., `arr[:] = arr.replace(...)`) because these methods return copies rather than mutating in place.

When a code path in `astropy/io/fits` produces no test failures after being commented out, treat it as a signal that the feature is untested and verify correctness by writing a targeted test before assuming the code is correct.

When fixing a silent no-op bug in FITS column formatting (such as D-exponent substitution in `_scale_back_ascii`), add a round-trip test that writes a FITS file with the relevant format code and reads it back to confirm the transformation was actually applied.

When investigating in-place vs. copy semantics for array operations in `astropy/io/fits/fitsrec.py`, check whether the target is a numpy `chararray` or `ndarray` slice, since slice assignment (`arr[:] = ...`) is required to mutate the underlying buffer rather than rebinding a local reference.

When encoding string literals for comparison or substitution against byte fields in `fitsrec.py`, prefer plain `b'...'` byte literals over `encode_ascii('...')` wrapper calls to reduce indirection and make the intent immediately clear.

When a WCS transformation function in `astropy/wcs/wcs.py` receives array inputs, check for empty arrays (zero size or zero in shape) before passing them to the underlying C library so that the C extension never receives degenerate input it cannot handle.

When wrapping low-level C/Fortran library calls (such as wcslib functions via `self.wcs.p2s` or `self.wcs.s2p`), add a short-circuit return of the input array unchanged whenever the input is empty, so callers get a consistent empty result instead of a cryptic native library error.

Avoid letting numpy broadcast or shape-validation logic run on zero-length arrays before checking for emptiness, because operations like `np.broadcast_arrays` and shape assertions can raise misleading errors that obscure the real cause (empty input) from the user.

When adding a guard for empty-input edge cases in coordinate transformation methods (`wcs_pix2world`, `wcs_world2pix`, `all_pix2world`, etc.), add parametrized tests that pass empty lists, empty numpy arrays, and zero-row 2-D arrays to every public transformation method to prevent regressions across the whole API surface.

When tracing a WCS transformation error, start at `_array_converter` in `astropy/wcs/wcs.py` since all public pixel↔world methods funnel through it via `_return_list_of_arrays` and `_return_single_array`, making it the single best place to add cross-cutting input validation.

When a Django setting defaults to `None` but a concrete value would prevent inconsistent behavior across code paths, set a sensible default in `django/conf/global_settings.py` so users get safe behavior without explicit configuration.

When a feature's behavior depends on which internal implementation path is taken (e.g., `MemoryUploadedFile` vs `TemporaryUploadedFile`), ensure the observable outcome is consistent regardless of that path so callers don't need to know implementation details.

When file permission issues arise on specific OS/Python combinations, check whether `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile` followed by `os.rename` is involved, since Python's `tempfile` module intentionally sets restrictive permissions (0o600) that survive the rename.

When changing a default setting value in `global_settings.py`, add or update tests that assert the new default is applied end-to-end (e.g., verify uploaded file permissions on disk) so regressions are caught if the default is reverted.

When tracing how an uploaded file's final permissions are set, follow the `FileSystemStorage._save` method in `django/core/files/storage.py` and the `FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS` setting consumption there to understand where a default change will take effect.

When a Django model field needs to support deferred evaluation, check the field's `formfield()` method in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` to find where stored attributes are passed to form classes, since that is the integration point where callables must be resolved.

When storing a configuration value on a model field that may vary by environment, avoid resolving it at class definition time; instead accept a callable and defer resolution to runtime so that migrations and form rendering use the correct value for each environment.

When tracing how a model field attribute flows into a form field, follow the `formfield()` override chain from `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` through any subclass, since each level may pass attributes directly to the form class constructor without further transformation.

When adding callable support to a field parameter, write tests that pass both a plain value and a callable returning the same value and assert identical behavior, ensuring the two code paths stay in sync as the codebase evolves.

When a field attribute is used in both `deconstruct()` and `formfield()`, apply the callable-resolution pattern (`value() if callable(value) else value`) only at the point of use rather than at storage time, so that `makemigrations` can still serialize the original callable reference instead of its resolved output.

When merging multiple ordered collections incrementally (as in `Media.merge`), avoid pairwise left-fold accumulation because intermediate results introduce spurious ordering constraints; instead, collect all lists and resolve order in a single pass using a topological sort.

When a module needs to merge items with ordering dependencies, use a dependency graph backed by `defaultdict(set)` and `OrderedSet` from `django.utils.datastructures` to represent and traverse constraints without losing insertion-stable ordering.

When a bug involves incorrect warnings or wrong output from a utility method, trace the call chain from the public API (e.g., `MyForm().media`) back through `_js`, `_css`, and `merge` in `django/forms/widgets.py` to find where intermediate state corrupts the final result.

When fixing a merge or ordering algorithm, write regression tests that combine three or more inputs whose pairwise merges would produce a different result than the full multi-way merge, to catch cases where incremental accumulation introduces false conflicts.

When detecting constraint violations (like `MediaOrderConflictWarning`), ensure the check operates on the full set of constraints simultaneously rather than on partial results, so that warnings reflect genuine conflicts in the original inputs rather than artifacts of evaluation order.

When a management command's behavior depends on database capabilities, check `connection.features` in `django/db/backends/base/features.py` to find the relevant feature flag rather than assuming uniform behavior across backends.

When a condition guards behavior in the migration executor (e.g., `MigrationExecutor` in `django/db/migrations/executor.py`), ensure the corresponding management command in `django/core/management/commands/` mirrors the same full condition rather than a subset of it.

When writing tests for database-feature-dependent behavior in `tests/migrations/test_commands.py`, mock the specific `connection.features` attribute (e.g., `can_rollback_ddl`) on an existing test rather than creating a new migration fixture, so the test stays focused on the feature flag itself.

When `sqlmigrate` output looks wrong, compare the condition in `Command.handle` inside `sqlmigrate.py` against the analogous condition in `MigrationExecutor` to spot any divergence between what the executor does and what the command reports.

When a boolean flag like `output_transaction` is derived from multiple independent conditions (migration atomicity and database DDL rollback support), always combine all conditions with `and` rather than relying on a single one, to avoid silently misrepresenting database behavior to the user.

When a view or middleware catches a specific exception type to handle error responses, check whether sibling exception classes (e.g., `Http404` vs `Resolver404`) share the same semantic intent, and catch the most appropriate one so callers can use the idiomatic Django API.

When tracing a bug related to HTTP error responses, start in `django/views/debug.py` where `technical_404_response` and similar helpers are defined, since that is where exception-to-response mapping is centralized.

Avoid catching a low-level internal exception (like `Resolver404`) in user-facing error handlers when a higher-level public exception (like `Http404`) is what application code is expected to raise, so the public API remains consistent and predictable.
When adding a new exception import to a module, verify the import list in that file is kept alphabetically ordered and grouped by package to match Django's existing style and avoid noisy diffs.

When fixing a mismatch between an expected exception type and a caught exception type, add a regression test that raises the previously-uncaught exception in the relevant code path and asserts the correct HTTP response is returned, so the behavior is locked in for future refactors.

When adding validation logic to model fields, locate the existing `_check_choices` or similar `_check_*` methods in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` to understand the pattern for returning `checks.Error` objects with unique `id` strings like `fields.E00X`.

When a field has both a constraint (like `max_length`) and a related attribute (like `choices`), add a cross-validation check in the field's `check()` pipeline that compares derived values from both attributes and returns a `checks.Error` if they are inconsistent.

When adding a new system check error, write tests that cover valid cases (no error raised), boundary cases (exact fit), and invalid cases (overflow), targeting the relevant test file in `tests/invalid_models_tests/` to match Django's existing check-testing conventions.

When iterating over `choices` that may contain grouped or flat entries, reuse the existing try/except unpacking pattern already present in `_check_choices` rather than writing a separate loop, so that edge cases like option groups and lazy strings are handled consistently.

When assigning a new `checks.Error` id, search `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` and the docs under `ref/checks.txt` for the highest existing `fields.E0XX` id to avoid collisions and maintain sequential numbering.

When serializing Python objects in `django/db/migrations/serializer.py`, prefer using an object's stable identifier (like `.name` for enums or a primary key) over its potentially mutable or translated value, so that serialized migrations remain valid across locale or data changes.

When a migration serialization bug is reported, locate the relevant serializer class in `django/db/migrations/serializer.py` by searching for the type name (e.g., `EnumSerializer`, `DatetimeSerializer`) and inspect how `serialize()` reconstructs the object, so you can identify whether it uses a stable or fragile representation.

When fixing a serializer in `django/db/migrations/serializer.py`, add a test in `tests/migrations/test_writer.py` that covers the edge case (e.g., an Enum with a translated or mutable value) to verify the serialized output uses the stable form and round-trips correctly.

When serializing an `Enum` member, use bracket notation (`EnumClass['NAME']`) rather than call notation (`EnumClass(value)`) so that the migration is keyed on the immutable member name rather than the potentially changing value.

When a migration raises `ValueError` about an unrecognized value at runtime, check whether the default was serialized via `EnumSerializer` in `django/db/migrations/serializer.py` using the enum's `.value` instead of `.name`, since translated or otherwise mutable values will break deserialization in other locales.

When investigating date/time parsing bugs in Django, start with `django/utils/http.py` where HTTP header parsing (dates, ETags, etc.) is centralized, so you can quickly locate the relevant logic without searching the broader codebase.

When implementing time-relative logic (e.g., two-digit year interpretation, expiry windows, or "recent" checks), avoid hardcoded cutoff values and instead derive thresholds dynamically from `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` so the logic stays correct as time passes.

When fixing date/time parsing that depends on the current year, write tests that compute expected values relative to `datetime.datetime.utcnow().year` rather than asserting against fixed years, so tests remain valid without modification over time.

When implementing RFC-specified date parsing in `django/utils/http.py`, cross-reference the relevant RFC (e.g., RFC 7231 for HTTP dates) directly in comments alongside the logic, so future maintainers can verify correctness against the spec without hunting for the source.

When a utility function in Django handles a format with multiple valid representations (e.g., two-digit vs. four-digit years in `parse_http_date`), ensure each branch derives its century offset from a shared dynamic baseline rather than independent hardcoded constants, so all branches stay consistent when the underlying assumption changes.

When tracing migration autodetection bugs, start in `django/db/migrations/autodetector.py` and follow the `generate_*` methods (e.g., `generate_altered_fields`, `generate_renamed_fields`) to understand how field state transitions are computed and where related field references may be missed.

When updating a field reference in a migration operation, update all dependent attributes together (e.g., both `remote_field.model` and `remote_field.field_name`) so that deconstruction methods like `ForeignKey.deconstruct()` produce consistent output rather than a mix of old and new state.

When a generated migration contains a stale field name in a `to_field` or similar parameter, check whether `autodetector.renamed_fields` is being consulted for all relevant rename keys, including the composite key that combines model name, field name, and remote field name.

When fixing a bug in migration autodetection, write a test in `tests/migrations/test_autodetector.py` that defines models with a renamed primary key and a referencing `ForeignKey`, then assert that the generated migration's `to_field` resolves to the new field name rather than the old one.

When investigating how `ForeignKey` serializes its arguments, read `ForeignKey.deconstruct()` in `django/db/models/fields/related.py` to understand which attributes (like `to_field`) are conditionally included, since that logic determines what the autodetector must keep consistent.

When investigating type coercion or string representation issues with Django model fields, start by examining `django/db/models/enums.py` and the `Choices`, `TextChoices`, and `IntegerChoices` class hierarchy to understand how enum values are wrapped and exposed.

When a class inherits from both a primitive type (like `int` or `str`) and `enum.Enum`, avoid relying on the default `__str__` from `enum.Enum` since it returns `ClassName.MEMBER_NAME` rather than the primitive value, which breaks template rendering and string comparisons.

When writing tests for model fields that use `choices`, assert both the type (`assertIsInstance`) and the string representation (`assertEqual(str(...), ...)`) on freshly created instances and on instances retrieved from the database, since the two code paths can behave differently.

When a model field value behaves differently depending on whether it was just assigned versus retrieved from the database, compare how the field's `from_db_value` and `to_python` methods (in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py`) handle the raw value versus the enum-wrapped value.

When adding a mixin base class (like `int` or `str`) to an enum subclass, explicitly define `__str__` to delegate to `self.value` so that the primitive type's string behavior is preserved and downstream code such as templates, serializers, and assertions receives the expected plain value rather than the enum repr.

When `contribute_to_class` in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` unconditionally calls `setattr` to install auto-generated methods on a model class, guard the call with `hasattr` so that user-defined overrides on the class or its parents are not silently clobbered.

When a model method behaves differently than expected, trace its installation site in `Field.contribute_to_class` rather than the method's runtime logic, since metaclass and field setup code can override user-defined methods before the class is fully constructed.

When a feature regresses between Django minor versions, diff the `contribute_to_class` and `contribute_to_class`-adjacent code paths in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` and `django/db/models/base.py` to identify where new `setattr` calls may have been introduced without existence checks.

When fixing a method-installation bug in `Field.contribute_to_class`, add a regression test that subclasses a model, explicitly defines the auto-generated method (e.g. `get_FOO_display`), and asserts that the subclass's version is called rather than the framework-generated one.

When using `partialmethod` or similar constructs to bind framework-generated methods onto model classes, always check whether the target attribute already exists on the class (not just its instances) so that inheritance and explicit overrides in user code are respected.

When investigating database routing or test isolation bugs, start by reading `django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py` and its `test_db_signature` method, since that method controls how Django deduplicates test database connections.

When a test database signature is computed, ensure all distinguishing attributes (such as the on-disk file path) are included in the tuple so that two connections to different physical files are never treated as the same database.

When a test fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked`, suspect that two separate database aliases are sharing a single connection due to a collision in `test_db_signature`, rather than assuming a concurrency or locking issue in the test itself.

When adding support for persistent or named SQLite test databases (via `TEST["NAME"]`), verify that the multi-database test suite (`admin_views.test_multidb`) passes with `--keepdb` and distinct file names for each alias, since that combination exercises the signature deduplication path.

When a Django project configures multiple SQLite databases with explicit `TEST["NAME"]` paths, confirm that each alias produces a unique `test_db_signature` tuple so the test runner does not incorrectly reuse one connection for both aliases.

When tracing how Python objects are serialized to migration files, start in `django/db/migrations/serializer.py` and identify which `Serializer` subclass handles the type in question, since each type has its own `serialize()` method that controls the generated string.

When generating a dotted import path for a Python class, use `__qualname__` instead of `__name__` so that nested or inner classes are represented with their full qualified name (e.g., `Outer.Inner`) rather than just the leaf name.

When a migration file contains an incorrect class reference, reproduce the issue by calling `MigrationWriter.serialize()` directly on the field or value in a shell session, which isolates the serialization logic from the full `makemigrations` command and makes the faulty output immediately visible.

When fixing a serialization bug involving class paths, add a regression test in `tests/migrations/test_writer.py` that serializes an inner class defined inside another class and asserts the output contains the fully qualified dotted path.

When referencing a class's location within a module for any dynamic import or code-generation purpose across the Django codebase, prefer `__qualname__` over `__name__` to correctly handle classes defined inside other classes, functions, or closures.

When a URL resolver produces unexpected argument counts, inspect `RoutePattern.match()` and `RegexPattern.match()` in `django/urls/resolvers.py` to verify how `groupdict()` and `groups()` interact before kwargs filtering strips values.

When filtering a dict to remove `None` values that represent optional captures, do so after using the unfiltered dict to decide between kwargs and positional args, so that the presence-check and the filtering operate on consistent data.

When fixing URL resolution bugs, add test cases in `tests/urlpatterns/` that cover optional named groups resolving to `None`, ensuring both the args/kwargs split and the final callback invocation are exercised.

When tracing how URL parameters reach a view, follow the call chain from `URLResolver.resolve()` through `RoutePattern.match()` / `RegexPattern.match()` into `ResolverMatch`, since that is where args and kwargs are assembled before dispatch.

When a regex URL pattern contains optional named groups, never conflate "no named groups matched" with "no named groups exist" — check `groupdict()` keys before filtering out `None` values so that optional params don't silently collapse kwargs into positional args.

When checking whether a method already exists on a class before setting it, use `cls.__dict__` instead of `hasattr(cls, ...)` so that inherited methods don't block the subclass from getting its own correctly-bound version.

When tracing how model methods like `get_FOO_display` are attached to a class, start in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` at the `contribute_to_class` method, which is where field-level class customization happens.

When a method returns unexpected results in a subclass that overrides choices or other field attributes, check whether `contribute_to_class` is skipping the `setattr` call due to an overly broad existence check that matches an inherited method rather than one defined on the subclass itself.

When fixing inheritance-related bugs on model fields, write regression tests that cover at least three levels: the base class behavior, the subclass with overridden attributes, and values that exist only in the subclass's extended definition.

When a field's behavior depends on class-level attributes that subclasses are expected to override (like `choices`), avoid using `hasattr` for guard checks in `contribute_to_class` since it conflates "defined here" with "reachable via MRO", which breaks the override contract.

When a check in `django/core/checks/` needs to validate language or locale settings, look for existing utility functions in `django/utils/translation/` (e.g., `get_supported_language_variant`) before implementing custom lookup logic, so the check reuses the same resolution rules the runtime uses.

When validating a setting against a set of allowed values, avoid simple membership tests on flat collections if the domain has hierarchical or fallback semantics; instead delegate to the authoritative resolution function so edge cases like sublanguage-to-base-language fallback are handled consistently.

When a validation check should pass if a fallback exists, wrap the resolution call in a try/except for the specific exception it raises (e.g., `LookupError` from `get_supported_language_variant`) and return the error only in the except branch, so the check mirrors actual runtime behavior.

When fixing a system check that incorrectly rejects valid configurations, add test cases in `tests/check_framework/` that cover both the sublanguage-with-available-base case and the genuinely invalid case, so regressions in either direction are caught.

When a `SystemCheckError` is raised for a setting that the runtime handles correctly at request time, compare the logic in the relevant `django/core/checks/` function against the runtime path in `django/utils/translation/` to find where the two diverge.

When a field type needs special rendering in the admin, look for existing `isinstance(field, ...)` branches in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py::display_for_field` to understand the pattern and insert new cases in the same structure.

When displaying field values in the admin, avoid calling `str()` or Python's default repr on field values directly; instead delegate to the field's own serialization method (like `get_prep_value` or `prepare_value`) so the output matches the field's expected format.

When calling a field's serialization method in `display_for_field`, wrap it in a try/except for the relevant exception type and fall back to `display_for_value` so invalid or unexpected inputs degrade gracefully rather than raising.

When fixing a display bug for a specific field type in the admin, write a test that renders a readonly `ModelAdmin` with that field and asserts the output is valid in the field's expected format (e.g., valid JSON for `JSONField`) rather than Python's repr.

When a form field has a `prepare_value` method and its model counterpart has `get_prep_value`, check both when fixing serialization mismatches, since the admin readonly path bypasses form rendering and needs the model-level method instead.

When saving multiple database objects in sequence that may have forward references or circular foreign keys, wrap the operation in `atomic(using=connection.alias)` so that constraint violations don't leave the database in a partial state.

When disabling constraint checks via `connection.constraint_checks_disabled()` to handle databases that don't support deferred checks (like MySQL), always follow up with an explicit `connection.check_constraints()` call so invalid data doesn't silently persist.

When tracing serialization/deserialization flows in Django, start from `django/db/backends/base/creation.py` — `serialize_db_to_string` and `deserialize_db_from_string` are the symmetric entry points for test database state management.

When deserializing and saving a collection of model objects from a fixture or snapshot, avoid saving each object immediately in a bare loop without a transaction, because insertion order may violate foreign key constraints that the serializer's dependency sort doesn't fully resolve.

When a `TransactionTestCase` subclass uses `serialized_rollback = True`, verify that the deserialization step handles cross-database-engine differences (e.g., MySQL vs PostgreSQL deferred constraint support) by testing against both engines rather than assuming one engine's behavior generalizes.

When investigating ordering bugs in ORM queries, start in `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py` at `find_ordering_name` and `get_order_by`, since these methods resolve field names to SQL ORDER BY clauses and are the central point where ordering logic can silently drop or invert direction.

When a method checks `field.attname != name` to detect a "direct field reference" and skip some fallback behavior, also check for semantic aliases like `pk` that map to the same field but won't match `attname`, so that the shortcut is treated identically to the concrete field name.

When a queryset produces unexpected ASC/DESC ordering, print `queryset.query` and trace the ORDER BY clause back through `SQLCompiler.find_ordering_name` to identify which branch is resolving the field, since the bug is usually a condition that misclassifies the field reference and falls through to a default ordering path.

When fixing an ordering bug involving model inheritance, write regression tests that assert both the SQL direction (via `str(qs.query)`) and the actual result order for the child model, covering `pk`, `-pk`, and the concrete primary key field name to ensure all aliases behave consistently.

When writing conditions that guard against applying a related model's default ordering in `find_ordering_name`, treat `pk` as a reserved shortcut that always refers to the model's own primary key rather than a relation, to prevent the relation-traversal branch from overriding an explicitly specified sort direction.

When investigating incorrect error messages or hints in Django's model validation, look in `django/db/models/fields/related.py` where `_check_relationship_model` and similar `_check_*` methods centralize field validation logic and their user-facing strings.

When writing hint text that references a Django field type by name, verify the field class matches the actual API being described so that users aren't directed to use the wrong field or pass arguments that don't belong to it.

When referencing keyword arguments in error hints or documentation, cross-check that each argument belongs to the field or class being named, since arguments like `symmetrical` and `through` are specific to `ManyToManyField`, not `ForeignKey`.

When a hint references version-specific behavior (such as `symmetrical=False` being required before Django 3.0), check the current Django version's changelog and release notes to determine if the requirement has been lifted and the hint needs updating.

When fixing incorrect error message text in model field checks, add or update tests in `tests/invalid_models_tests/` that assert the exact hint string so regressions in user-facing guidance are caught automatically.

When a SQL alias conflicts with a column name from a JOINed table, check `query.alias_map` in `django/db/models/sql/query.py` to enumerate joined models and their concrete fields, then avoid using the alias in GROUP BY so the database can resolve the reference unambiguously.

When generating GROUP BY clauses in `set_group_by`, never use an annotation alias directly if that alias string matches any column name present in joined tables, since databases like PostgreSQL will treat the bare name as ambiguous between the alias and the column.

When investigating GROUP BY or annotation SQL generation bugs, start in `django/db/models/sql/query.py` at `set_group_by` and `get_group_by_cols`, then trace how `annotation_select` aliases are passed down to compiler methods in `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py`.

When fixing a query-generation bug that only surfaces with a specific combination of annotations, subqueries, and JOINs, write a regression test that constructs the full queryset chain (including `OuterRef`, `Subquery`, `Count`, and `values().annotate()`) and asserts the rendered SQL contains a fully-qualified column reference rather than a bare alias in the GROUP BY clause.

When iterating over `self.alias_map` to inspect joined tables, skip the first entry (the base table) using `list(self.alias_map.values())[1:]`, because the base table's columns are the ones being selected and should not be treated as collision candidates for GROUP BY alias resolution.

When investigating data sanitization gaps in `django/views/debug.py`, trace the `cleanse_setting` method's type-dispatch logic to identify any iterable or container types not explicitly handled, so that nested sensitive values are not silently passed through.

When writing recursive data-cleansing logic, avoid handling only `dict` while ignoring other container types like `list` and `tuple`, since sensitive values nested inside those structures will be returned unredacted.

When adding sanitization coverage for `SafeExceptionReporterFilter`, write tests that nest sensitive keys inside lists and tuples at multiple depths, so that regressions in recursive cleansing are caught before release.

When extending type-dispatch branches in a cleansing or filtering function, preserve the existing `TypeError` catch around the entire block so that non-iterable edge cases continue to fall back to the safe default rather than raising.

When a security-sensitive utility like `cleanse_setting` is modified, cross-check all call sites in `django/views/debug.py` (such as `get_safe_settings` and `get_safe_request_meta`) to confirm the fix propagates to every place that surfaces user-visible data.

When adding validation for a new constraint or option type, locate the existing `_check_*` methods in `django/db/models/base.py` and follow their patterns so the new check integrates consistently with the system check framework.
